prompt: A stop-and-wait protocol sends 1250-byte frames over a 100 Mbit/s link with a 10 ms RTT. Ignoring ACK transmission time, what is its link utilisation? Here RTT means propagation round trip; ignore processing, losses, ACK transmission and framing gaps.

options.explanation: That would be true if the RTT were tiny compared with the frame time. Here the sender spends 0.1 ms sending and 10 ms waiting.
This assumes sending and waiting take the same time. The wait (10 ms) is 100 times the frame time (0.1 ms).
This is off by a factor of ten. Check the frame time: 10,000 bits at 10⁸ bit/s is 0.1 ms, not 1 ms.
Correct. The frame takes 0.1 ms to send and the sender then waits 10 ms, so it is busy 0.1 / 10.1 ≈ 0.0099 of the time.

workedExample:
Each cycle: send one frame, then wait a round trip for the ACK.

```formula
L = 1250 B × 8 bit/B = 10,000 bit
L / R = 10,000 bit / (10⁸ bit/s)
L / R = 0.0001 s = 0.1 ms
U = (L / R) / (L / R + RTT)
U = 0.1 ms / (0.1 ms + 10 ms)
U = 0.1 / 10.1 ≈ 0.0099 = 0.99%
X = L / (L / R + RTT)
X = 10,000 bit / 10.1 ms ≈ 1 Mbit/s
where
L: the frame size, in bits
B: bytes; bit/B is bits per byte (8)
bit: one binary digit; bit/s is bits per second
R: the link rate, 100 Mbit/s = 10⁸ bits per second
s: seconds
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
U: the utilisation: the fraction of time the sender is transmitting
RTT: the round-trip propagation delay, 10 ms
X: the throughput: one frame per cycle
Mbit/s: megabits per second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the sender transmits for 0.1 ms and then waits 10 ms, so the link is busy only about **0.99%** of the time and carries about 1 Mbit/s of a 100 Mbit/s link.
```

Pipelining, with many frames in flight, is the fix.
